question:
(i) Explain how Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment led to the conclusion that an atom has a small, positively charged nucleus.
(ii) Why does the observation that only a very small fraction of alpha particles are scattered through large angles support the small size of the nucleus?

options.A:
(i) Since all alpha particles passed straight through the foil, Rutherford concluded that there is no positive charge inside an atom.
(ii) Large-angle scattering by nearly all alpha particles proves the nucleus fills almost the whole atom.
options.B:
(i) Most alpha particles passed undeflected, showing atoms are mostly empty space. A few large deflections and rare rebounds showed strong repulsion from a concentrated positive charge, so nearly all positive charge and most mass lie in a tiny nucleus.
(ii) Only a very small fraction undergoes large-angle scattering because the positively charged nucleus occupies a very small volume compared with the atom.
options.C:
(i) Rutherford concluded that electrons are concentrated at the atom's centre and alpha particles are attracted to it.
(ii) The small fraction of large deflections means positive charge is uniformly spread across the atom.
options.D:
(i) Alpha scattering showed that an atom is a solid sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded inside.
(ii) Few large deflections prove the nucleus is larger than the atom.
